name: State
intent: Let an object change its behaviour when its internal state changes, by delegating to a state object.
scenario: A document moves through Draft, Review and Published. What publish(), reject() and edit() do depends on which state it is in.
problem: Every method on the document starts with if/else on a status string: if status is draft... else if review... The same set of states is repeated in every method, and each new state means editing all of them. Invalid transitions are easy to miss.
solution: Create one class per state, each implementing publish(), reject() and edit() for that state only. The document holds a current state object and delegates every call to it. A state changes the document's state when a transition happens.
pain: Every method repeats an if/else over the status string
A new state means editing every method
Invalid transitions are easy to forget
The rules for one state are scattered across the class
benefits: Each state's rules live in one small class
A new state is a new class, not edits everywhere
Invalid actions are rejected in the state that forbids them
The document delegates: publish() is one line
whenToUse: An object behaves differently depending on its state, with many states
State-specific if/else is duplicated across methods
Workflows, order status, connection lifecycles, UI modes, game character modes
whenNotToUse: There are only two simple states: a boolean may be clearer
State rarely changes or behaviour barely differs
A lookup table of transitions is simpler than classes
pitfalls: Many small classes for a small state machine
Transition logic spread across states can be hard to see as a whole
States may need a lot of access to the context's data
Easy to confuse with Strategy: states change themselves, strategies are chosen by the client

roles.label: Context
roles.description: Holds the current state and delegates behaviour to it.

roles.label: Concrete State
roles.description: Behaviour for one state, including transitions.

quiz.question: An Order class has pay(), ship() and cancel(), and each starts with an if/else on a status string. The team adds a Refunded status, edits five of the six branches, and an order in Refunded can now be shipped. Which change removes this class of bug?
options: Move each status into its own class, with the order delegating each call to the current one
Replace the status string with an enum and keep the if/else chains in each method, checking cases in order
Add a unit test that runs ship() once for every status value
Put the status checks in one validate() method that every action calls first
quiz.explanation: With one class per state, the rules for Refunded live in a single place and ship() there simply rejects. An enum or a shared validate() still keeps the status checks in the order class, so a new state can still be missed. A test catches this one case but not the next.

quiz.question: A network Connection moves through Connecting, Open and Closed, and close() or an error means different things in each. In the State pattern, who decides that an Open connection becomes Closed after a socket error?
options: The caller, which picks the state to use before each call
The connection class, using a switch over a status field
The Open state object, which sets the next state
A separate scheduler that polls the connection and rewrites its state
quiz.explanation: In State, the current state object handles the event and sets the context's next state, so the connection only delegates. Caller selection describes Strategy. A switch in the connection brings back the conditional logic the pattern is meant to remove.

quiz.question: A payment workflow has 12 states and 5 events. In every state, the only differences are which events are legal and which state comes next. No state has its own logic, and the rules change monthly. Which design is the simplest that works?
options: Twelve state classes, each with five methods that repeat the same rejection code
A transition table that maps state and event to the next state, held as data
One long if/else per event over the current state, written inside the workflow class
A strategy object per event, picked by the caller from the current status
quiz.explanation: When states differ only by legality and next state, a table is shorter, easier to review and easy to change, and State classes add little. Twelve classes repeat boilerplate. If/else chains and caller-chosen strategies scatter the same table through code.
